Modify a Hessian

Source: R/modify.R
hessian_modify.Rd

Generic that returns a positive definite matrix \(\tilde H\) in place of a Hessian \(H\) for which the Cholesky factorization failed. newton() and chebyshev() solve \(\tilde H d = -g\) for the direction. There is one method for each hessian_modification() subclass; a new modification is a subclass and a method, and newton() needs no change.

Usage

hessian_modify(modify, H)

Arguments

modify

A hessian_modification() object.

H

A symmetric numeric matrix.

Value

A numeric matrix with the dimension of H, intended to be positive definite.

Requirements on a method

The method receives the modification object and the Hessian \(H\), a symmetric numeric matrix with finite entries, and returns a numeric matrix of the same dimension. The returned matrix should be positive definite: the method of the optimizer solves with it, and a direction that is not a descent direction is replaced by a scaled gradient step, which is recorded in the trace as hessian solve failed. A returned matrix of another dimension or with non-finite entries is treated in the same way. The method is called only at an iterate at which \(H\) is not positive definite, and is called from compiled code through R, once per such iterate.

Writing a modification

A modification is defined by (1) a subclass of hessian_modification() with the parameters of the rule as properties, (2) a constructor that sets the label shown when the optimizer is printed, and (3) a method for this generic, registered with S7::method(). The shipped classes modify_eigen() and modify_ridge() are handled in compiled code; any other class, including a subclass of one of them, is called through this generic.

References

Dauphin, Y. N., Pascanu, R., Gulcehre, C., Cho, K., Ganguli, S. and Bengio, Y. (2014). Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 27.

See also

hessian_modification(), modify_eigen(), modify_ridge(), modifications, newton(), chebyshev()

Examples

# The shipped methods, on an indefinite matrix with eigenvalues 2 and -1.
H <- matrix(c(0.5, 1.5, 1.5, 0.5), 2, 2)
eigen(H, only.values = TRUE)$values
#> [1]  2 -1
hessian_modify(modify_eigen(floor = 0.1), H)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  1.1  0.9
#> [2,]  0.9  1.1
hessian_modify(modify_ridge(), H)
#>          [,1]     [,2]
#> [1,] 1.842177 1.500000
#> [2,] 1.500000 1.842177

# A user-defined modification: replace each eigenvalue by its absolute
# value, with a lower bound (the saddle-free Newton method of Dauphin et
# al., 2014). Unlike the eigenvalue floor, it uses the magnitude of a
# negative curvature as the curvature of the quadratic model.
ModifyAbs <- S7::new_class("ModifyAbs", parent = hessian_modification,
  properties = list(floor = S7::class_numeric))

modify_abs <- function(floor = 1e-8) {
  ModifyAbs(label = paste0("absolute eigenvalues (floor = ", floor, ")"),
            floor = floor)
}

S7::method(hessian_modify, ModifyAbs) <- function(modify, H) {
  e <- eigen(H, symmetric = TRUE)
  e$vectors %*% (pmax(abs(e$values), modify@floor) * t(e$vectors))
}

hessian_modify(modify_abs(), H)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  1.5  0.5
#> [2,]  0.5  1.5

# The new object is passed to newton() like a shipped one, here on the
# Himmelblau function, started where its Hessian is not positive definite.
k <- test_problems("himmelblau")[[1]]
eigen(k$he(c(0.5, 0.5)), only.values = TRUE)$values
#> [1] -20.05573 -37.94427
r <- minimize(newton(modify = modify_abs(), keep_trace = TRUE), k$fn,
              c(0.5, 0.5), gr = k$gr, he = k$he)
c(value = r@value, iterations = r@iterations, converged = r@converged)
#>        value   iterations    converged 
#> 3.346705e-24 7.000000e+00 1.000000e+00 
unique(r@trace$safeguard)
#> [1] "hessian modified (capped)" "none"
